title: Protein Shake for a Hangover: Before, During, and After Drinking
excerpt: Does a protein shake help a hangover? When it's worth drinking one (before, with, or after alcohol), how to build a stomach-friendly shake, and what it can't fix.
metaDescription: Does a protein shake help a hangover? When to drink one before, with, or after alcohol, what to put in it, and what protein can and can't fix.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a protein shake won't cure a hangover, but it can be a genuinely useful tool at two points in the night. Before you drink, a shake with some carbs and fat in it puts food in your stomach, which slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream. The morning after, a gentle shake is often easier to get down than a full plate when you're queasy, and it can deliver fluid, protein, and (if you add fruit or oats) the carbohydrates your blood sugar is asking for. What a protein shake can't do is "absorb" alcohol, speed up how fast your liver clears it, or undo the effect a heavy night has on muscle recovery.

**The quick rules:** Drink a shake with carbs and some fat in it 30 to 60 minutes before you go out, rather than on an empty stomach. Don't mix protein powder into alcoholic drinks expecting protection. The morning after, make it smaller and blander than usual, use water or a lactose-free base if your stomach is upset, add a banana or oats for carbs, and sip it slowly alongside plain water. Skip caffeinated "pre-workout" powders and products heavy in sugar alcohols while you're hungover.

> **When to see a doctor.** A hangover is uncomfortable but it should be getting better through the day, not worse. **Get medical help** if you can't keep any fluids down for many hours, you're vomiting blood or something that looks like coffee grounds, you have severe or worsening stomach pain, chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that won't settle, confusion, seizures, or you're so drowsy that you're hard to wake. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, dangerous dehydration, or something other than a hangover. If someone is unresponsive, breathing slowly or irregularly, or having a seizure, call 911 (or your local emergency number). If you regularly feel shaky, sweaty, or anxious the morning after drinking and those feelings ease when you drink again, talk to a doctor about it; that pattern can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal rather than an ordinary hangover.

## Does a Protein Shake Actually Help a Hangover?

It helps in some ways, and it's oversold in others. The useful thing to know is what a hangover actually is, because that tells you what a shake can and can't touch.

A hangover isn't one problem. Researchers describe it as a cluster of effects that show up as your blood alcohol falls back toward zero. The main drivers include:

- **An inflammatory response.** Alcohol triggers your immune system, and higher levels of inflammatory signaling molecules have been linked to worse hangover symptoms.
- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver turns alcohol into acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product, before breaking it down further into harmless acetate.
- **Disrupted sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments sleep in the second half of the night.
- **Fluid loss and an irritated stomach.** Alcohol makes you urinate more, and it irritates the stomach lining and increases acid.
- **Low blood sugar in some people.** While your liver is busy with alcohol, it's worse at making new glucose, which can leave you shaky, weak, and foggy, especially if you didn't eat.

Look at that list and you can see where a protein shake fits. It does nothing for inflammation, acetaldehyde, or broken sleep in any direct way. It can help with fluid (it's mostly liquid), it can help with blood sugar (if you build it with carbs, since protein alone does little here), and it can be gentle on a sore stomach (if you pick the ingredients carefully). The biggest value actually comes earlier, before you start drinking.

It's also worth clearing up a myth. You'll sometimes hear that protein "soaks up" or "absorbs" alcohol. It doesn't. Alcohol is a small molecule that passes into the blood from your stomach and small intestine. Food of any kind slows this down mainly by keeping alcohol in your stomach longer, not by binding to it. Protein is one useful part of that meal, but it isn't magic.

## Protein Shake Before Drinking: The Most Useful Time

If you only use a protein shake at one point in the night, make it before you go out. This is where the evidence is strongest, and it's about food in general rather than protein specifically.

### Why food before drinking matters

When your stomach is empty, alcohol moves quickly into your small intestine, where it's absorbed fast. Your blood alcohol rises sharply and peaks higher. When you've eaten, a valve at the bottom of your stomach (the pylorus) stays closed longer while your stomach digests the meal. Alcohol sits in the stomach for longer, more of it gets broken down there before it ever reaches your blood, and what does get absorbed arrives more gradually.

Studies going back decades, including controlled work by the Swedish forensic researcher A.W. Jones and colleagues, have shown that drinking after a meal produces a noticeably lower peak blood alcohol than drinking the same amount on an empty stomach. A lower, slower peak tends to mean you feel less wrecked and make better decisions about the next drink. Our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) covers this in more detail.

### Does protein work better than other food?

There's no good evidence that protein beats other nutrients at slowing alcohol absorption. Protein, fat, and fiber all slow the rate at which your stomach empties, and a mixed meal containing all three seems to be the practical sweet spot. The studies that show the biggest effect generally used real meals, not single nutrients.

That's actually the main point for shake drinkers: **a scoop of whey in water is a very light snack.** It leaves your stomach relatively quickly and doesn't contain much fat or fiber. It's better than nothing, but it isn't the same as a meal. If you want your pre-drinking shake to do real work, make it more like a meal in a glass.

### A better pre-drinking shake

Build your shake with:

- **Protein:** one normal serving of your usual protein powder (most people use about 20 to 30 grams of protein).
- **Fat:** a tablespoon of peanut butter or almond butter, a spoonful of chia seeds, or whole milk rather than water. Fat is one of the strongest slowers of stomach emptying.
- **Slow carbs and fiber:** a handful of rolled oats, a banana, or some berries.
- **Liquid:** milk, a milk alternative, or water.

Drink it 30 to 60 minutes before your first drink. If you're going straight to dinner, the dinner does the job and the shake is optional. If you're heading out with nothing in your stomach, which happens a lot after work or the gym, this is where a shake earns its place. For more ideas, see our guide on [what to eat before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-eat-before-drinking-alcohol-evidence-based-guide).

### What it won't do

Even a perfect pre-drinking shake only slows absorption. It doesn't reduce the total amount of alcohol you take in, and over a long night most of that alcohol still ends up in your blood. Six drinks after a protein shake are still six drinks. The shake buys you a gentler curve, not a free pass.

## Protein Shake With Alcohol: Mixing Them in the Same Glass

Some people ask about adding protein powder to cocktails, or drinking a "boozy protein shake." It's an occasional fitness-community trend, especially with cream liqueurs, vodka, or rum blended into a chocolate or vanilla shake.

Here's what's actually going on:

- **The protein and fat may slow absorption slightly**, the same way food does, because they keep the drink in your stomach longer. That's not a reason to do it, but it's not harmful either.
- **It doesn't protect your liver or your muscles.** Your liver still has to process the same amount of alcohol. The protein doesn't change that.
- **Creamy, sweet drinks hide alcohol.** A thick shake with a couple of shots in it tastes like dessert. It's easy to drink more than you planned, and harder to judge how strong it is. Know how many standard drinks are in the glass; our page on [what counts as a standard drink](/never-hungover/what-is-a-standard-drink) can help.
- **Dairy plus alcohol can upset some stomachs.** If you're even mildly lactose intolerant, a large dairy shake with alcohol can lead to bloating, cramps, or diarrhea the next day.

If you like a protein shake on a night out, the more useful pattern is to drink it before you start, then stick to your normal drinks, alternating with water.

### What about during the night?

Snacking during a long night out helps in the same way that eating beforehand does: it keeps something in your stomach. If a shake is the easiest thing to get, it's a reasonable choice. A plate of real food is usually better, and water between drinks matters more than either.

## Protein Shake After Drinking: The Morning After

This is the moment most people actually search for, and it's where a shake can be a smart, low-effort move, as long as you make the right kind.

### Why a shake can make sense when you're hungover

- **It's easy to get down.** Many people with a hangover can't face a plate of food. A cold, thin, mild-tasting drink is often more manageable than chewing anything.
- **It provides fluid.** A shake is mostly liquid. Research on how well different drinks keep people hydrated has found that milk tends to be retained in the body better than plain water, probably because of its protein, sodium, and potassium content. A well-known 2016 study by Maughan and colleagues, which created a "beverage hydration index," found milk scored higher than water over the hours after drinking. That doesn't make milk a treatment for a hangover, but a milk-based shake isn't a bad source of fluid if it agrees with your stomach.
- **It can bring your blood sugar back up**, if you add carbs. Protein alone does relatively little here. A banana, some oats, honey, or fruit makes the shake much more useful.
- **It delivers protein you might otherwise skip.** If you'd normally eat a solid breakfast and you're likely to skip it, a shake helps you avoid going until the afternoon without any real food.

### The cysteine question

You'll sometimes see claims that protein helps a hangover because it contains **cysteine**, an amino acid your body uses to make glutathione, a key antioxidant in the liver. There's a grain of truth here. Whey protein is relatively rich in cysteine, and a small Finnish study published in 2020 in the journal *Alcohol and Alcoholism* reported that people taking L-cysteine supplements had milder hangover symptoms in some measures than people taking a placebo.

But that study was small, it used a concentrated supplement rather than food, and it hasn't been widely repeated. There's no good evidence that the cysteine in a scoop of whey makes a meaningful difference to how your hangover feels. Treat it as a nice bonus at most, not the reason to drink a shake.

### How to make a hangover-friendly shake

A morning-after shake should be gentler than your usual post-gym shake:

1. **Go smaller.** Half to one normal scoop is plenty. A huge, thick shake can sit heavy in an already irritated stomach.
2. **Choose a gentle base.** Water, coconut water, oat milk, or lactose-free milk tend to be easier than regular milk if you're queasy. If dairy is normally fine for you and your stomach feels okay, milk is a reasonable choice.
3. **Add carbs.** A ripe banana is the classic choice: it's soft, easy to digest, and adds potassium. Rolled oats, a little honey, or frozen berries also work. Our page on [bananas for a hangover](/never-hungover/bananas-for-hangover) goes into why they're a common pick.
4. **Add a pinch of salt if you've been sweating or vomiting.** It sounds odd, but a small pinch of salt in a fruit shake is barely noticeable and helps replace sodium.
5. **Keep it bland.** Vanilla or unflavored usually goes down better than intense chocolate or "birthday cake" flavors when you're nauseated.
6. **Sip it slowly** over 15 to 20 minutes, alongside plain water or an electrolyte drink.

A simple version: one scoop of vanilla protein, one banana, a small handful of oats, a pinch of salt, ice, and a cup of oat milk or water. For more blends, see our [hangover smoothie recipes](/never-hungover/hangover-smoothie-recipes).

### What to avoid in a hangover shake

- **Caffeinated or "pre-workout" protein products.** Many contain a lot of caffeine plus stimulants. On top of a hangover, that can make a racing heart, jitteriness, and anxiety worse.
- **Lots of sugar alcohols.** Sweeteners like sorbitol, maltitol, and erythritol are common in protein products and bars. In larger amounts they can cause gas, bloating, and diarrhea, which is the last thing an alcohol-irritated gut needs.
- **High-fat, very thick shakes if you're nauseated.** Fat is great before drinking, because it slows your stomach. The morning after, that same slowing can make nausea feel worse. Keep the nut butter light until your stomach settles.
- **Acidic add-ins if you have heartburn.** Orange juice and lots of citrus can aggravate acid reflux, which alcohol already makes more likely.
- **Adding more alcohol.** The "hair of the dog" idea just delays the hangover. There's no good evidence that it helps, and it adds to the total load on your body.

### What if you can't keep anything down?

If you're vomiting, don't force a shake. Start with small sips of water or an oral rehydration drink, wait until you've kept those down for an hour or so, then try something bland. Our [hangover nausea guide](/never-hungover/hangover-nausea-complete-guide-fast-stomach-relief-2025) walks through a step-by-step approach. If you can't keep fluids down for many hours, that's a reason to see a doctor, not to try harder with food.

## Protein Shake vs. a Real Breakfast

A shake is convenient, but it's rarely better than real food when you can manage it.

| | Protein shake | Solid hangover breakfast |
|---|---|---|
| Easy to get down when queasy | Usually yes | Often harder at first |
| Fluid | Yes, a good amount | Little, unless you drink alongside |
| Protein | Yes, easily 20 to 30 grams | Yes, with eggs, yogurt, or meat |
| Carbs for blood sugar | Only if you add fruit or oats | Toast, potatoes, oats, fruit |
| Salt and electrolytes | Little, unless you add them | Often more (eggs, toast, broth) |
| Keeps you full | Moderately | Usually longer |

A sensible approach: start with a small shake and some water if your stomach is unsettled, then move to real food once you feel up to it. Eggs are a popular choice because they're a solid source of protein and are easy to cook; see our post on [eggs for a hangover](/never-hungover/eggs-for-hangover). Our guide to the [best hangover breakfast](/never-hungover/best-hangover-breakfast) has more options that balance protein, carbs, and salt. For the full list, see our guide to the [best foods for a hangover](/never-hungover/best-foods-for-hangover).

## Protein Shakes, Alcohol, and Muscle Recovery

A lot of people searching this topic are gym-goers who are worried that a night out undid their training. That concern is fair, and this is where a protein shake gets the most attention from researchers.

### What the research found

A frequently cited 2014 study by Parr and colleagues, published in *PLoS ONE*, looked at a small group of physically active men who did a hard training session and then drank a large amount of alcohol (roughly a heavy night out). The researchers measured muscle protein synthesis, which is the process your body uses to repair and build muscle.

The main findings were:

- **Alcohol after training reduced muscle protein synthesis**, even when the men also had protein.
- **Having protein alongside the alcohol softened the drop**, compared with having alcohol with carbohydrates only, but it didn't bring recovery back to normal.

The study was small, used a heavy dose of alcohol, and only included men, so it's not the final word. But the direction is clear and matches other research: heavy drinking after a workout blunts recovery, and a protein shake partly, but not fully, offsets that.

### What that means in practice

- **If you train on the day you plan to drink, have your protein after training anyway.** It's still better than skipping it.
- **The amount of alcohol matters more than the shake.** One or two drinks is very different from a heavy session. The research effects come from heavy drinking.
- **Don't plan to "earn" the drinks with a shake.** The protein doesn't cancel out the alcohol.
- **The morning after, protein is still useful**, because recovery continues over the following day or two.

For a deeper look, see our guide on [alcohol, protein synthesis, and muscle recovery](/never-hungover/alcohol-protein-synthesis-muscle-recovery-impact-guide-2025).

### Should you work out the morning after?

Light movement, like a walk, is fine for many people and can help you feel more awake. A hard workout while dehydrated, short on sleep, and possibly still affected by alcohol is a different story. Your coordination and reaction time may be off, your heart rate may already be raised, and you're more likely to get hurt. If you do train, keep it easy, drink plenty of water, and have your shake afterward. Our article on [whether exercise helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-exercise-help-a-hangover) covers this in more detail.

## Which Protein Powder Is Best for a Hangover?

There's no protein powder made specifically for hangovers that has good evidence behind it. The best choice is mostly about what your stomach tolerates.

- **Whey isolate.** Very low in lactose and digests fairly quickly. A good option if regular milk products bother you but you prefer dairy protein.
- **Whey concentrate.** Contains more lactose than isolate. Fine for many people, but more likely to cause bloating if you're sensitive.
- **Casein.** Digests slowly. Arguably better before drinking (slower stomach emptying) than the morning after, when it can feel heavy.
- **Plant proteins (pea, soy, rice, blends).** Lactose-free and often well tolerated. Some people find the texture grittier, which can be off-putting when you're nauseated.
- **Ready-to-drink protein shakes.** Convenient when you can't face a blender. Check the label for caffeine and sugar alcohols.

Whatever you choose, use one you already know agrees with you. A hangover morning isn't the time to try a new product.

## Common Mistakes With Protein and Hangovers

- **Treating a shake as a full meal before drinking.** A scoop in water is a snack. Add fat, fiber, and carbs if you want it to slow absorption.
- **Skipping carbs the morning after.** If you feel shaky, weak, or foggy, low blood sugar may be part of it. Protein alone won't fix that; fruit, oats, or toast will help more.
- **Forgetting water.** A shake adds fluid, but it doesn't replace drinking water steadily through the morning. See our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).
- **Grabbing a caffeinated protein drink.** Extra stimulants on a hangover can make your heart race and leave you more anxious.
- **Making it huge.** A big, thick, fatty shake on a sore stomach can bring on nausea.
- **Expecting protein to cure the hangover.** It supports recovery. Time, sleep, fluids, and food are what actually get you through it.

## Taking a Wider View: Preventing the Next One

A protein shake is a reasonable part of a night-out routine, mostly as a pre-drinking snack and a gentle morning-after option. But the things with the most impact are still the basics: eat a real meal before drinking, pace yourself (about one standard drink an hour or slower), alternate alcohol with water, and stop earlier than you think you need to. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

Some people also add a supplement to their routine. **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of that research comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data, so it's best viewed as promising rather than proven. It isn't a substitute for food, water, or drinking less, and there's no good evidence that it lets you drink more without consequences. If you'd like to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people typically take and when. If you take any prescription medicines, check with a pharmacist or doctor before adding a supplement.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is a protein shake good for a hangover?**

It can help, but it isn't a cure. The morning after, a small, bland shake is often easier to get down than solid food, and it provides fluid and protein. Add a banana or oats for carbohydrates, since low blood sugar can be part of feeling shaky and foggy. Sip it slowly alongside water, and skip caffeinated or heavily sweetened products.

**Should I drink a protein shake before drinking alcohol?**

Having food in your stomach before drinking slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood and lowers the peak. A shake can do that job if you make it more like a meal, with some fat (nut butter or whole milk) and fiber or carbs (oats or a banana). A scoop of protein in water alone is a light snack and will have a smaller effect. A real meal is better still.

**Can you mix protein powder with alcohol?**

You can, and it won't hurt you in itself, but it doesn't protect your liver or your muscles. The protein and fat may slow absorption a little, the same way food does. The bigger risk is that creamy, sweet drinks hide the alcohol, so it's easy to drink more than you planned. Count the standard drinks in the glass.

**Does protein absorb alcohol?**

No. Alcohol isn't soaked up by protein. Food of any kind slows absorption mainly by keeping alcohol in your stomach longer, where some of it is broken down and the rest reaches your blood more gradually. Protein is a useful part of a pre-drinking meal, but fat, fiber, and carbohydrates help just as much.

**Does drinking alcohol ruin my protein shake after the gym?**

It reduces the benefit but doesn't cancel it. A 2014 study by Parr and colleagues found that heavy drinking after training lowered muscle protein synthesis, and having protein with the alcohol softened that drop without bringing it back to normal. Have your protein after training anyway, and keep in mind that the amount you drink matters more than the shake.

**What should I put in a protein shake for a hangover?**

Keep it simple and gentle: half to one scoop of a mild protein powder, a ripe banana or a handful of oats, a pinch of salt if you've been sweating or vomiting, ice, and water, oat milk, or lactose-free milk. Avoid pre-workout or caffeinated powders, products high in sugar alcohols, lots of citrus if you have heartburn, and very thick, fatty blends while you're nauseated.

**Is whey or plant protein better for a hangover?**

Neither has evidence of being better for hangovers specifically. Choose the one your stomach handles best. Whey isolate is very low in lactose, plant proteins are lactose-free, and whey concentrate contains more lactose and may cause bloating in sensitive people. A hangover morning is not the time to try a new product.

**Can a protein shake replace breakfast when I'm hungover?**

It can stand in for breakfast if you can't face solid food, but real food usually covers more of what you need, including salt and carbohydrates, and keeps you full longer. A good pattern is to start with a small shake and water while your stomach settles, then eat something like eggs and toast once you're able.
